case_study_insert.main_stem: Redpine Ski Resorts (RSR) is a public limited company in the tourism and leisure sector, employing a workforce of 85. Founded in 1994 by Anika Berg, it operates three alpine ski lodges and uses a flat structure with democratic leadership. RSR plans to invest $1,200,000 in a new high-speed cable car, financed by a $700,000 ten-year bank loan and $500,000 from a share issue. It has fixed costs of $1,500,000 a year, a variable cost of $90 per visitor-day and a selling price of $240 per visitor-day, and currently produces 45,000 units a year. RSR faces two problems: lift downtime is rising and ski-equipment defect rates have climbed to 3.4%.
case_study_insert.appendix_1_marketing_ops: Resort Operations and Guest Survey, Winter 2025: RSR recorded 12,400 visitor-days across its three lodges, with lift downtime averaging 14 hours a month, up from 8 hours a year earlier. Ski-equipment defect rate reached 3.4% and guest complaint cards rose from 31 to 52 per month. A survey of 700 visitors found 61% would pay $20 more for guaranteed lift reliability and 49% would rebook only if queues are short. Average lift queue time was 18 minutes. Technician retraining on the new cable-car system costs $700 per employee.

appendix_2_financial_data.title: Extract from the Statement of Financial Position of Redpine Ski Resorts as at 31 March 2025 ($ '000)

case_study_insert.appendix_3_external_environment: Economic and Tourism Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank has raised the base interest rate from 4.5% to 5.25%, raising borrowing costs for resorts with variable-rate loans. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 6.0% from $12.40 to $13.14 per hour from April 2026. (3) Lift-maintenance and energy input costs have risen 8.7% year-on-year, while inbound tourism spending grew 5.2% and inflation is 6.1%.

questions.question_text: RSR plans to fund part of its $1,200,000 cable car through a share issue. Explain two advantages for RSR of using this share issue rather than the bank loan.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: The $500,000 raised from a share issue does not have to be repaid and carries no mandatory interest, unlike the $700,000 ten-year bank loan whose cost rises with the base rate now at 5.25%. This strengthens RSR's cash flow while it already carries $1,500,000 fixed costs, so more of the $150 contribution per visitor-day can be spent on cutting the 14 hours of monthly lift downtime rather than on debt service.

Point 2: Equity widens RSR's shareholder base without putting its $5,600,000 of non-current assets at risk of repossession if the new cable car fails to attract the 61% of surveyed visitors who would pay $20 more for reliability. As a public limited company, RSR can access many investors, and the fresh capital also improves the equity cushion shown in its financial position, making future borrowing for the lodges easier. Existing shareholders dilute their control, but the democratic leadership style can manage that trade-off.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation applied to RSR's financing and expansion.

questions.question_text: RSR wants to attract skiers to its new cable car. Consider sponsoring a national ski champion, targeted email marketing to past guests, or winter sports magazine advertising. Which should RSR choose? Justify your recommendation.
questions.model_answer:
Sponsoring a national ski champion: Association with a champion would build credibility and excitement around the high-speed cable car and reach the winter-sports community quickly. It is expensive, however, and the endorsement lasts only while the athlete stays prominent; for a business servicing a $700,000 loan and spending $1,200,000 on the cable car, the fee could be hard to justify, and it does not directly target past guests who already know RSR's three lodges.

Targeted email marketing: Emailing the past guests who make up much of the 12,400 visitor-days is cheap, measurable and personal, and can promote the 61% of surveyed visitors willing to pay $20 more for reliability. Its limit is reach: it cannot attract new skiers beyond the existing database, so it cannot by itself lift the 45,000 visitor-day target or counter the 49% who rebook only when queues are short.

Winter sports magazine advertising: Print adverts reach committed skiers across the country and suit a premium, reliability-focused message. Yet readership is falling, the lead time is long, and there is no measurable response, which is a problem when lift downtime is already 14 hours a month and guests must be convinced quickly.

Recommendation: RSR should choose targeted email marketing, supported by small social posts. It is low-cost, precisely reaches the guests behind 45,000 visitor-days, and can highlight the new cable car to the 61% who value reliability. Champion sponsorship is rejected as costly and transient given the $700,000 loan; magazine advertising is rejected as slow and unmeasurable compared with the 5.2% growth in inbound tourism.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Limited outline of the promotional options with minimal application to RSR.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Discussion of advantages and disadvantages of at least two options in RSR's context with some judgement.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three options in RSR's context with a justified recommendation explaining why the other two are rejected.

questions.question_text: RSR's lift downtime is rising and equipment defects have reached 3.4%. Explain two benefits for RSR of its democratic leadership style in addressing these problems.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Democratic leadership invites the 85 employees, especially lift technicians, to share ideas about why downtime averages 14 hours a month. In a flat structure, their practical suggestions can be acted on quickly, reducing breakdowns and helping deliver the 61% of surveyed visitors who would pay $20 more for guaranteed lift reliability, while protecting the 12,400 visitor-days recorded last winter. Fewer breakdowns also protect the $240 price because fewer refunds are needed.

Point 2: Consulting staff about the 3.4% ski-equipment defect rate gives them ownership of quality checks, so faults are reported early rather than hidden. Greater involvement raises motivation and commitment, which can reduce the 52 monthly complaint cards and lower the $700-per-employee retraining cost on the new cable-car system, as experienced technicians pass on their knowledge willingly. With 85 staff across three lodges, that local ownership reduces the need for head-office intervention. Reliable lifts also support the 5.2% growth in inbound tourism that RSR is trying to capture.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid benefit identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual explanation linked to RSR downtime, defects and staff.

questions.question_text: RSR must upskill technicians to maintain the new cable car. Consider on-the-job training or off-the-job training at the technical college. Which should RSR choose? Justify your decision.
questions.model_answer:
On-the-job training: Learning beside the existing lifts is directly relevant to RSR's own equipment and keeps technicians productive, which helps cut the 14 hours of monthly downtime and the 3.4% defect rate without losing operating days. It costs no course fees and suits the flat structure. However, trainers pass on their own habits, formal certification is limited, and a safety-critical cable car may require documented qualifications that on-the-job coaching cannot provide.

Off-the-job training: The technical college course at $700 per employee gives structured, up-to-date skills and a recognised certificate for the technicians, which matters for a public limited company operating a new high-speed cable car. It also brings outside expertise on fault diagnosis that can tackle the 52 monthly complaints. The costs include fees and time away from the lifts, and the generic content may not cover RSR's exact machines, so follow-up coaching is still needed, and 14 hours of monthly downtime is costly in lost visitor-days, so training speed matters.

Decision: RSR should choose off-the-job training for safety certification, followed by short on-the-job sessions. The flat structure lets technicians bring course ideas straight to managers. Formal qualifications protect guests and the $1,200,000 investment, while the 6.0% wage rise makes the $700 per employee a worthwhile once-off. On-the-job training alone is rejected because it cannot supply the certification a safety-critical cable car demands, even though it is cheaper and less disruptive. With 5.2% inbound growth, the resort cannot afford a safety failure on a flagship cable car. Certificates also reassure the 61% of guests who pay more for reliability.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Basic description of the two training methods with limited application to RSR.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed analysis of benefits and drawbacks of both training methods in RSR's context.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Comprehensive evaluation of both methods with a justified decision covering safety, cost and relevance.

questions.question_text: Calculate and explain how RSR's management can use its cost, break-even and productivity data.

sub_parts.model_answer: Formula: Break-even output = Fixed costs ÷ Contribution per unit. Substitution: $1,500,000 ÷ ($240 − $90) = $1,500,000 ÷ $150 = 10,000 units. Answer: break-even output is 10,000 visitor-days a year.
Formula: Contribution per unit = Selling price − Variable cost per unit. Substitution: $240 − $90 = $150. Answer: contribution per unit is $150.

sub_parts.question_text: Explain four ways RSR's management can use this financial data.
sub_parts.model_answer:
1. RSR can compare the 10,000 visitor-day break-even with actual 45,000 visitor-days, a margin of safety of 35,000, to see how far winter bookings can fall before losses begin while the cable car is installed.
2. The $150 contribution lets managers test the survey finding that 61% would pay $20 more: if all visitor-days gained $20, contribution would be $170 and break-even $1,500,000 ÷ $170 = 8,824 visitor-days, showing reliability's value.
3. Managers can use break-even to set the volume needed to service the $700,000 loan alongside $1,500,000 fixed costs, checking the 45,000 visitor-day forecast before committing further expansion.
4. Average total cost of $1,500,000 ÷ 45,000 + $90 = about $123.33 per visitor-day can be tracked each month to reveal the 8.7% lift-maintenance and energy inflation early, guiding the $700 technician training spend.

questions.model_answer: (i) Break-even output = 10,000 visitor-days | (ii) Contribution per unit = $150 | (iii) Four contextual uses explained: margin of safety against 45,000 visitor-days; $20 reliability premium and break-even of 8,824; loan-service target; and average total cost of $123.33 to track 8.7% input inflation.

working_marks: 1 mark for correct formula/method, 1 mark for accurate numerical answer in (i) and (ii). 1 mark per valid applied point in (iii).

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 2, evaluate RSR's financial position by calculating the current ratio and the acid test ratio for 2024 and 2025. Has RSR's financial position improved? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Calculations:
Current Ratio 2024 = 1.60 : 1
Current Ratio 2025 = 1.47 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2024 = 0.80 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2025 = 0.81 : 1

Detailed workings: 2024 current assets = $240,000 inventories + $150,000 trade receivables + $90,000 cash = $480,000; 2025 current assets = $210,000 + $200,000 + $60,000 = $470,000. Short-term cover 2024 = $480,000 ÷ $300,000 = 1.60; 2025 = $470,000 ÷ $320,000 = 1.47. Excluding stock, 2024 = ($480,000 − $240,000) ÷ $300,000 = $240,000 ÷ $300,000 = 0.80; 2025 = ($470,000 − $210,000) ÷ $320,000 = $260,000 ÷ $320,000 = 0.81.

Evaluation: The picture is mixed and, overall, not an improvement. Short-term cover fell from 1.60 to 1.47 because current liabilities rose from $300,000 to $320,000 while current assets slipped from $480,000 to $470,000; cash fell from $90,000 to $60,000 even as receivables rose from $150,000 to $200,000. That means more wealth is tied up in unpaid guest and tour-operator invoices, which may not arrive before the $700,000 loan instalments. The stricter test improved only marginally, from 0.80 to 0.81, because inventories were also reduced, so the resort is still heavily reliant on stock and on collecting debts to meet near-term obligations.

Conclusion: RSR's financial position has not clearly improved. The main measure fell, and the small rise in the stricter measure is too slight to offset higher liabilities and lower cash, especially with $1,200,000 being spent on the cable car. Credit control over the $200,000 receivables should be tightened before further borrowing.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: States financial figures without accurate ratio calculations.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Accurately calculates both ratios for both years with contextual analysis of the trend.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Accurate calculations for both years with detailed evaluation of cash, receivables and liabilities and a justified conclusion on RSR's financial position.

questions.question_text: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for RSR of introducing quality control inspections on its hired ski equipment.
questions.model_answer:
Advantage: Inspection can catch the faults behind the 3.4% defect rate before guests collect their equipment, reducing the 52 monthly complaint cards and supporting the 61% of surveyed visitors who would pay $20 more for reliable service. Fewer breakdowns also cut the 14 hours of monthly lift disruption, protecting the $150 contribution per visitor-day and the 45,000 visitor-day target; at 12,400 visitor-days last winter, even a small fall in defects protects real revenue.

Disadvantage: Inspection adds staff time and cost at a moment when input prices have risen 8.7% and a $700,000 loan is being serviced, potentially pushing up the $1,500,000 fixed costs. Checks can slow the rental process and lengthen the 18-minute queue, which matters because 49% of visitors rebook only if queues are short; if faults are still missed, the $1,200,000 cable-car investment gains little benefit. The 49% who rebook only if queues are short may also be put off if checks slow rentals.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for a valid advantage and 1 mark for a valid disadvantage.
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual development linked to RSR's defect rate, complaints and costs.

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the interest rate rise to 5.25%, the 6.0% minimum wage increase and the 8.7% rise in lift-maintenance and energy costs will affect RSR. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Interest rate rise (4.5% to 5.25%): If RSR's $700,000 loan is variable-rate, the 0.75 percentage point rise adds 0.75% × $700,000 = $5,250 a year, a modest sum against $1,500,000 fixed costs; if the loan is fixed, there is no direct increase. Higher rates could raise the cost of financing the $1,200,000 cable car and cool the 5.2% growth in inbound tourism, but fixing the rate would cap much of this.

Minimum wage increase (6.0%, to $13.14 per hour): With a workforce of 85 across three lodges, wage costs rise and cannot be avoided. No hours or individual pay are given, so an annual wage total cannot be invented; the defensible comparison is productivity — 45,000 visitor-days ÷ 85 staff = about 529 visitor-days per employee. If the cable car raises throughput, the extra pay is absorbed; if downtime stays at 14 hours a month, the $150 contribution per visitor-day is squeezed.

Lift-maintenance and energy costs (+8.7%): These feed the $90 variable cost per visitor-day. As a clearly labelled upper bound, if all $90 rose 8.7% that is $7.83 per visitor-day (8.7% × $90), or roughly $352,350 a year at 45,000 visitor-days. Even a partial rise cuts contribution, and the $20 reliability premium wanted by 61% of guests can recover only part of it.

Conclusion: The 8.7% input-cost rise will have the greatest impact. It applies to every visitor-day, directly erodes the $150 contribution that funds the cable car, and recurs each year, whereas the interest effect is small and fixable and the wage effect depends on productivity gains from the new lift.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the external factors with limited application to RSR.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two external changes on RSR's costs, revenue or financing in context.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three external changes in RSR's context with a well-justified judgment that input-cost inflation has the greatest impact and why the other two are smaller.
